en: When it comes to
extending the capabilities of AI agents,
another core concept is the concept of agent
skills. Now,
agent skills in a nutshell are just Markdown
files.
And Markdown in turn is just a way of
formatting plain text. So in the end, we're
talking about plain text files formatted in
a certain way.
And the idea behind agent skills is simply
just that there is a relatively standardized
way of naming and storing those Markdown
files such that AI agents can automatically
discover it.
Because the idea is that you could set up
skills that describe certain workflows or
maybe the usage of certain software or tools
that may exist on your system
such that AI agents can work with them more
efficiently.
You can think of agent skills simply as
reusable prompts in the end, because again,
they are just plain text files. The idea
just is that you as the user of an AI agent
software, of the ChatGPT application, for
example, that you can write your knowledge
or your instructions that you want the agent
to follow in certain situations into such a
skill file.
And then the skill file will be loaded
automatically by that application and will
be sent to the agent automatically so that
you don't manually have to repeat your
instructions over and over again. Now,
what's very interesting about this
standardized agent skills concept is that
you don't just have that reusable piece of
information, that reusable prompt that's
sent to the agent in the end, but that it's
also based on a system where you have a
brief description of what that skill is
about in some metadata that's attached to
the skill file.
And initially, those AI agents only load all
those descriptions of all the skills that
are available to them.
And that then allows the AI model to make
decisions on which skills to fully load for
a certain task it may be tackling right now.
So that if you're using an AI agent to, for
example, help you with both accounting and
software development, you may have different
agent skills for these different areas. But
you, of course, don't want to load all skill
files for every prompt you're sending to the
agent because that would simply take up
space in the context window and it would
send information to the agent that's not
relevant to the task, which is always a bad
idea. So instead, this agent skill standard
requires the setup or the existence of a
short description in every skill file. And
that description then allows the agent and
the underlying model, which is used as a
brain, to smartly make decisions for which
skill files to load in full based on the
concrete task you then gave it. So that if
you're asking an agent to help you with
accounting,
it only loads the accounting-relevant skills
and not the skills related to software
development, for example.
And that's therefore another concept to be
aware of that depending on which AI agent
you're working with, you may be able to
define such skill files, store them in
predefined locations that may differ based
on which agent you're using, The official
documentation is the way to go, of course.
And then the agent can load and activate
those skills as needed to have extra
information defined by you that help it
perform certain tasks in a better way than
it maybe was able to do before.
